reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry meets the difficulty head-on, distinguishing Genesis 6:5's "continually" (aggravated, ongoing sin) from 8:21's "from his youth" (innate weakness), which excuses rather than aggravates.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the point bluntly: God destroys life for human evil in 6:5-7, then cites the same evil as reason never to repeat it.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, comment on Genesis 8:21 (skepticsannotatedbible.com/gen/8.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; gen/8.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: But the reason of this resolve is very surprising, for it seems the same in effect with the reason given for the destruction of the world: Because the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth, Gen 6:5. But there is this difference - there it is said, The imagination of man's heart is evil continually, that is, "his actual transgressions continually cry against him;" here it is said, It is evil from his youth or childhood.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry names the exact tension the row raises — v. 21's reason looks 'the same in effect' as Gen 6:5's — then resolves it by distinguishing 'evil continually' (aggravated, ongoing transgression, the flood's ground) from 'evil from his youth' (innate condition, now a ground for forbearance).

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), p. 68
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under the heading 'Will destroy. / Will not destroy,' Haley pairs Genesis 6:7's "I will destroy man whom I have created" against Genesis 8:21's "Neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done," and resolves it as two time-bound declarations — "One of these utterances was made before, the other after, the Flood. Both declarations were strictly fulfilled."
